aliases: one rule for how to live
entry_question: Who decides the right way for someone to live? Is an official answer possible?
text: A name helps you point something out. It does not settle every question about it. Before accepting one official answer for how a person should live, ask whose life it describes and whose it leaves out.
title: The Way That Can Be Named

text: The person who truly knows how to do a thing often doesn't look flashy while doing it. Showing all your strength at once usually means you are not sure it is there. Clumsy-looking isn't clumsy; it is just not spending energy on the surface. The show-off is the tired one, because he has to keep proving himself. The one who doesn't force it keeps that energy to get the thing done.
title: Great Skill Looks Clumsy

text: Picture a seedling on the windowsill. If the soil is dry, water it. Once it has enough water, leave the roots alone. Acting without forcing means helping where help is needed, not sitting there doing nothing.
title: Acting Without Forcing

text: Water gives roots a drink and runs into the low places nobody is fighting to occupy. It helps without asking to be put first. That is the part of water worth imitating.
title: The Highest Good Is Like Water

text: Is losing always bad? Is winning always good? Today's luck may be carrying tomorrow's trap, and today's stumble may push you onto an easier road. So don't be quick to stamp a thing good or bad. Give it a little time before you decide what it was.
title: Fortune and Misfortune Lean on Each Other

text: Hui could not lift his giant gourd full of water. Cut into dippers, it was still awkward. Zhuang suggested floating on it instead. When you say something is useless, what job did you have in mind for it?
title: The Use of the Useless

text: Two people argue over who is right, and usually each is standing in his own spot, neither seeing where the other stands. Right and wrong always come with a position. Instead of forcing a single answer, put both positions on the table and see where they differ. Once you can see that, the either-or loosens on its own.
title: Right and Wrong Depend on Where You Stand

text: From the bridge Zhuangzi sees fish swimming at ease. Huizi asks how someone who is not a fish could know the fish are happy. Are they describing what they see, or claiming to know how it feels from inside? Those are different questions.
title: The Happiness of Fish

text: Cook Ding lets the blade pass through the spaces between the joints instead of driving it into bone. At a difficult spot he slows down and looks again. Before pushing harder on a task, see whether there is another opening.
title: Cook Ding Carves the Ox

entry_question: Does dreaming mean the world is unreal? What can a dream actually prove?
text: In his dream, being a butterfly felt perfectly ordinary. Awake, he was Zhuang Zhou again. The story asks what changes when the one doing the looking changes. It is a question about perspective, not proof that nothing is real.
title: Zhuang Zhou and the Butterfly

text: The harder you scramble for first place, the more you collide with others. Rivers and seas sit low, and that is why every stream flows toward them. Not contending is not giving up; it is refusing to stand at the front as a target. Make room, and the thing gets done without leaving enemies.
title: Not Contending

text: You don't keep flipping a small fish; flip it too much and it falls apart. Leading a team works the same way. Once the direction is set, don't change it daily or meddle in everything. A good leader is like the pan: enough heat, few turns, let the thing cook itself. The less you churn it, the steadier it gets.
title: Governing a Large State Is Like Cooking a Small Fish

text: A carpenter wants straight boards. A gnarled tree is no use to him for that. For the tree, being passed over means a chance to live. To someone resting in its shade, it is useful already. Whose use are we counting?
title: A tree the carpenter passes by

text: If the same paragraph has begun to blur, put the draft down for a while. When you come back, read just that paragraph. Is there something that needs changing, or has changing it become a habit?
title: Putting the draft down

text: You could ask your friend, “What happened from where you stood?” You might still disagree. At least you will be talking about what happened, instead of trying to make each other feel small.
title: A quarrel with a friend

text: No. Making room for different standpoints is not the same as requiring one opinion. If I loosen my grip on my own view, I have a chance to hear yours. Neither of us has to turn into the other.
title: Must everyone agree?

text: Your hand holds the clay, but the soup goes in the space the clay leaves open. A wheel needs a hole for its axle, and a room needs openings. The material and the empty space do different jobs.

text: Chapter seven asks why heaven and earth last so long. Neither lives for its own sake. The sage follows their example: his own place is not his first concern, yet he does not lose it.

text: The spokes meet at a hub, but the axle needs the hole. A pot needs its hollow; a room needs doors and windows. The material gives the thing its shape. What is not filled in lets us use it.
title: What makes a wheel or a room useful?

text: It takes force to prevail over someone else. Can you also master yourself? The chapter sets those strengths alongside one another, then asks what wealth means to someone who already has enough.

text: Listen for what a speaker can stand behind, not just what sounds pleasing. The chapter ends with another contrast: the sage acts for others without making a contest of it.

text: Water reaches living things by flowing into places that people avoid. The comparison is not about a flood winning a fight. It is about giving something useful without competing for the best position.
title: What water does in the low places

text: In the marsh the bird has to walk for each bite and go farther for a drink. A full trough would save it trouble. The story asks us to notice something the trough cannot offer: the bird never asked to live in a coop.
title: Would the marsh pheasant choose the coop?

text: You can point to the wood that has burned away. That does not tell you where the fire will end: it has already passed on. The closing image leaves the end of the fire open.
title: Does the flame end with one log?

text: At Lao Dan’s death, Qin Shi cries out three times and leaves. A disciple questions his friendship. Qin Shi answers by speaking of a time to come and a time to go, not by measuring friendship in tears.
title: Why did Qin Shi leave the funeral?

text: Chapter eight, in our translation from the classical text: “The highest good is like water. Water benefits the myriad things without contending.”
title: Water in chapter eight: what does the text say?

text: In our translation of the classical passage: “The marsh pheasant takes ten steps for a peck, a hundred for a drink. It has no wish to be kept in a cage. Even if its spirits flourished there, it would be no good.”

text: The carpenter passes the crooked tree. No straight boards there. But a traveller can lie down in its shade. Before you call the tree worthless, whose use of it have you counted?
title: What a carpenter leaves standing

text: The opening chapter turns from names to a difference in attention. When desire falls quiet, the subtle comes into view. When desire is present, the outlines come into view. The two looks need not point to two different worlds.
title: What changes when you look with desire?
A name is not the person
text: A label helps you point someone out; it cannot finish describing them. You do not have to give up words. When a label stops helping and starts replacing the person, set it down for a moment and look again. Think of one time the label fit, then one time it did not. You can keep using the words "difficult person", then ask what this particular person actually did. If a more accurate word shows up, use it. The point is not silence; it is not mistaking the word for the person.

text: Lay a stick beside a twig, then beside a beam. Is the stick long or short? Neither answer belongs to it alone. The same passage sets before and behind in a pair: one position makes sense through the other.
title: How can long and short define one another?
Who set the standard, and who takes the credit
text: Call one thing beautiful and you have already picked a standard; a different standard may bring out a strength the first one misses. Before you rank two people, ask what you are actually comparing. Judging is not forbidden: races need timing, hiring needs tests. What needs watching is the moment ranking turns people into grades: one red flower handed out, and the child without it becomes "the unkind one." And when something was made together, you do not have to push one person forward to own all the credit. Do the thing, help it along, then step back. If the work holds up without your name on it, that is a stronger finish than a plaque.

text: Chapter nineteen does not end with a list of things to reject. It turns to what a person can keep: simplicity, fewer private aims, and fewer wants. Dropping a public show of virtue need not mean dropping the care a family needs.
title: What comes after the three refusals?
When the trappings crowd out the point
text: Would one more title, one more layer of packaging, make the thing itself better? Packaging changes with the season while the inside stays the same; slogans sound fine while the work goes hollow. Try dropping one frill and see whether the work still serves the people it was for. You do not have to stop learning or stop caring for others, and this is not a ban on buying what you need. One test: if nobody were watching and no reward were attached, would you still do it? Keep whatever survives that question. Drop the trappings, not the care. Wanting to prove you are better than others is also a frill; it can be dropped too.

title: Chapter 1 in plain English
text: A way you can put into words is not the constant way. A name you can give is not the constant name. Before names, heaven and earth had just begun; with names, the ten thousand things have a mother. So: keep wanting nothing, and you see the subtlety that usually slips past; keep wanting something, and you see where things show their edges. The two come out of one source and only differ in what we call them. Both are called deep. Deeper than deep: that is the door the wonders come through.

title: Chapter 2 in plain English
text: Everyone knows what beauty is: ugliness is already there. Everyone knows what good is: what is not good is already there. So having and not-having give each other birth; hard and easy complete each other; long and short shape each other; high and low lean on each other; sound and voice harmonize; front and back follow. That is why the sage dwells in the work of not-doing and teaches without words. The ten thousand things rise, and he does not refuse them. He gives life without owning, does the work without leaning on it, finishes without dwelling in the finish. Precisely because he does not dwell in it, it does not leave.

title: Chapter 19 in plain English
text: Drop the sage and throw away cleverness, the chapter says, and the people gain a hundredfold. These three, it says, are not enough as mere ornament, so give people somewhere to belong: show the undyed silk, hold the uncarved wood, keep private aims few and wants fewer.

text: What is most complete can look unfinished, yet use never wears it out. What is fullest can look empty, yet use never exhausts it. Think of a pot on the shelf. How well does it pour?

title: Chapter 50 in plain English
text: Out is life; in is death. Those who belong to life: three in ten. Those who belong to death: three in ten. And those who, living, move into the ground of death: also three in ten. Why? Because they make their living too thick. I have heard that one who is good at keeping life, walking on land, does not meet the rhinoceros or the tiger, and entering the army, is not touched by armor or blade. The rhinoceros finds no place to throw its horn, the tiger no place to set its claws, the blade no place to admit its edge. Why? Because he has no ground of death.

title: Chapter 55 in plain English
text: One who holds virtue thick is like a newborn child. Wasps and scorpions and vipers do not sting him; fierce beasts do not seize him; birds of prey do not strike him. His bones are soft and his sinews supple, yet his grip is firm. He knows nothing of the joining of male and female, yet he rises, the utmost of essence. He can cry all day and not grow hoarse, the utmost of harmony. Knowing harmony is called the constant; knowing the constant is called clear-sighted. Piling up life past what is called for is called a portent; letting the heart drive the breath is called forcing. When a thing is grown strong, it grows old: that is called not the Way, and what is not the Way ends early.

title: Chapter 56 in plain English
text: Those who know do not speak; those who speak do not know. Block the openings, shut the doors, blunt the sharpness, untie the tangles, soften the glare, merge with the dust; this is called the dark unity. So you cannot get close to him, and cannot keep him at a distance; cannot profit him, and cannot harm him; cannot exalt him, and cannot degrade him. Therefore he is valued by the world.

title: Chapter 57 in plain English
text: Use uprightness to govern the state, surprise to wage war, and no business to win the world. How do I know it is so? By this. The more restrictions and taboos in the world, the poorer the people; the more sharp weapons among the people, the darker the state; the more skill and cleverness among people, the more strange things arise; the more laws and orders are proclaimed, the more thieves and robbers there are. So the sage says: I do not act, and the people transform themselves; I love stillness, and the people straighten themselves; I keep out of business, and the people enrich themselves; I am without desires, and the people return to plainness.

title: Chapter 58 in plain English
text: When the government is muffled and dull, the people are simple and honest; when the government is sharp and probing, the people are sly and wanting. Calamity: that is where fortune leans. Fortune: that is where calamity hides. Who knows where it ends? There is no fixed rule. The straight flips into the sly; the good flips into the monstrous. People have been lost in this for a long, long time. So the sage is square without cutting, edged without wounding, straight without being reckless, bright without dazzling.

title: Chapter 59 in plain English
text: For governing people and serving heaven, nothing is like thrift. Only thrift is called early preparation; early preparation is called piling up virtue. Piling up virtue, there is nothing you cannot overcome; overcoming everything, no one knows your limit. With no limit known, you can hold the state; with the mother of the state, you can last long. This is called deep roots and a firm base, the Way of long life and lasting sight.

title: Chapter 60 in plain English
text: Governing a great state is like cooking a small fish; do not keep turning it. Rule the world with the Way, and the ghosts lose their power. Not that the ghosts lose their power, but their power cannot harm people. Not only does their power not harm people; the sage does not harm people either. When neither harms the other, virtue settles back where it belongs.

title: Chapter 61 in plain English
text: A great state is like the low ground downstream, the meeting point of the world, the female of the world. The female always wins the male by stillness; by stillness she stays below. So a great state, by lowering itself to a small state, wins the small state; a small state, by lowering itself to a great state, wins the great state. So some lower themselves to win, and some lower themselves and are won. A great state wants nothing more than to shelter many people; a small state wants nothing more than to enter and serve. When each gets what it wants, the greater one should do the lowering.

title: Chapter 62 in plain English
text: The Way is the depth of the ten thousand things. It is the treasure of the good person and the shelter of the person who is not good. Fine words can be traded; honored conduct can be added to a person. As for those who are not good, why throw them away? So when the Son of Heaven is installed and the three ministers are set up, though one offers a disc of jade and a team of horses, it is better to sit still and offer this Way. Why did the ancients prize this Way? Do they not say: sought, and it is found; guilty, and it is forgiven? So it is prized by the world.

title: Chapter 63 in plain English
text: Do the not-doing; work at the unworked; taste the tasteless. Small is where big begins, few is where many begins; repay resentment with virtue. Take the hard in hand while it is easy; take the big in hand while it is small. The hard things of the world must be done while they are easy; the great things of the world must be done while they are small. So the sage never makes himself big, and so he is able to complete his bigness. A light promise is seldom kept; much easiness turns into much difficulty. So the sage treats things as hard from the start, and in the end has no difficulty.
